These counsels were given to a community with no state, no courts of its own and very little power, which is worth noticing: they were offered as wisdom to be lived rather than as a system to be enforced. The commentators treat the bracket as deliberate. Mecca's objection was never to good conduct, which its own tribes prized, but to the exclusive claim that stands at both ends of the passage.

keyTerms.note: The root carries the sense of a bridle: what restrains and steers. Wisdom in this vocabulary is not accumulated information but the capacity to place a thing correctly, which is why counsels can be called by the name.
A verb for communicating quickly and privately, used of a hint or a signal as well as of revelation. It describes transmission that is direct and unobserved rather than a text handed over in public.

From a verb for pushing something off. The same word closes an earlier ayah in this surah about a life aimed only at the immediate, which links the two failures by their outcome rather than their content.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wisdom literature was familiar in Arabia. Proverbs, maxims and the sayings of famous judges circulated by memory, and a man known for sound judgement was consulted across tribal lines. What was strange in this passage was not its advice, much of which any elder would have endorsed, but its attribution. These were not the accumulated conclusions of experience. They were being described as sent.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for wisdom occurs exactly once in this surah, and it occurs here, applied backwards to the counsels just given rather than forwards to anything new. Nothing in that run is called law or command; it is named as wisdom disclosed. The classical commentators note that the label covers the whole passage, not only the ayah it sits in.
studies.theologicalSignificance: By calling the preceding counsels a portion of wisdom, the ayah refuses to present them as exhaustive, which leaves the moral life larger than any list. And by closing the frame where it opened, it makes ethics dependent on attachment rather than the reverse. The order matters: the passage does not argue that right conduct leads to right belief. It presents the whole run of counsels as what a single loyalty looks like when it is lived out.

crossReferences.why: Opens the same frame in identical words, at the other end of these counsels.
Calls wisdom an abundant good, given to whomever God wills, and rarely grasped.
Gives another run of counsels bracketed the same way, from a father to his son.

studies.applyIt: Read the ayat between the two brackets in one sitting, without stopping to study them. Parents, relatives, the poor, the traveller, speech, spending, children, honesty, the scale. Notice that they arrive as a list and not as a system, and that they are described as a portion of something larger. Then pick the one you skipped over fastest, and sit with that one instead.

studies.title: Sons For You, Daughters For Him
studies.meaning: The argument is made by holding two Meccan beliefs together until they collide. The same men who considered a daughter a misfortune assigned daughters to God, and called the angels female. The ayah does not attack the low view of daughters directly; it uses it, asking whether God has kept for Himself what they would not want. The verdict is delivered in a single phrase about the size of the statement. The following ayah observes that the argument has been turned every way, and that turning it only increases the recoil.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Several Arabian tribes regarded certain angels as daughters of God, and the Quran returns to this claim repeatedly in the Meccan period, each time pressing the same inconsistency. The same society is described elsewhere as receiving the birth of a daughter with shame. The commentators read these ayat within the surah's argument about the Quran's reception rather than tying them to a single reported occasion.

keyTerms.gloss: has He then chosen for you
keyTerms.note: The verb means to select the pure part of a thing, the way cream is skimmed. It sharpens the question: are you saying He kept the residue for Himself and skimmed the best off for you.
A verb for rotating something so it can be seen from every side, also used of shifting winds. It describes the Quran restating one case in many forms rather than repeating itself.
The word used of a camel shying and running from something that startles it. It makes the reaction physical and involuntary rather than a considered reply to the argument being made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sons carried the tribal name, fought, inherited and defended the well. Daughters married outward, and their marriages moved property and honour into another house. A man's standing in the assembly was counted partly in sons. That arithmetic was so ordinary it went unspoken, which is what makes the ayah's manoeuvre effective: it does not have to explain the preference, only to point at where it had been quietly applied.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran raises this same inconsistency in at least four separate Meccan surahs, each time by contrast rather than by direct denial, and one of those places asks the question in almost the same words as this one. The strategy is consistent: the claim is dismantled by the objectors' own valuation instead of by an argument they would have to accept first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attacks a way of thinking rather than a doctrine. Attributing offspring to God projects human continuation onto Him, and the ayah exposes the projection by showing that the projectors did not even project their own best. It also establishes something about revelation in the line that follows: clarity is not what produces acceptance. The same turning of the argument that opens one hearer is described as driving another further off.

crossReferences.why: Sets the attribution beside the father's darkened face at the news of a daughter.
Ties the naming of angels as female to disbelief in the Hereafter specifically.
Asks whether they witnessed the angels' creation, and says the claim will be recorded.

studies.applyIt: Catch yourself, once today, doing what this ayah exposes: holding two standards without noticing. What you accept in yourself and refuse in someone else, or what you demand of a stranger and excuse in a friend. Do not fix it and do not feel bad about it. Just find one, and say what it is. The argument here works by making people see their own arithmetic written down.

studies.title: They Would Have Sought A Way
studies.meaning: The argument is short and turns on a single consequence. If other gods existed alongside Him, they would have looked for a route to the Throne, because power that is real does not sit quietly beside a greater power. Commentators read the seeking in two ways: as rivalry, or as the lesser gods themselves seeking nearness to the true one. Either reading leaves the Meccan position incoherent, since their gods neither contended nor drew near. The second ayah answers not with a further argument but with a declaration of distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Meccans did not deny God; they held that lesser powers had a share, and approached them for intercession and for local needs. The Quran's Meccan arguments therefore aim less at the existence of God than at the coherence of a hierarchy with junior partners. The commentators place this ayah in that debate, and no specific occasion is attested for it beyond the standing dispute at the sanctuary.

keyTerms.note: The ordinary word for a road. Its plainness is the point: the ayah does not describe a metaphysical relation but a path someone would take, which is what any genuine power would look for.

The image names sovereignty rather than furniture, and the classical commentators are careful to say so, treating it as the seat of authority over creation without describing anything a person could picture.

keyTerms.gloss: and He is exalted far above
keyTerms.note: From the root of height, and the same root the surah used earlier of an arrogance that rises against others. Here the height is God's, which is the one place the word carries no fault at all.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca understood power as hierarchy. Tribes had chiefs, alliances had senior and junior partners, and everyone knew that a strong client eventually pressed against his patron. Nobody in that world believed two forces could hold real power in one place indefinitely without one testing the other. The ayah puts its case in terms the assembly used every week about their own arrangements.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran makes this argument from the incoherence of divided power at least three times, in three different Meccan surahs, and each version turns on a different consequence: seeking a way to the Throne, the ruin of the heavens and the earth, and each god carrying off what it had made. The conclusion is the same; no two of them run the same route to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage argues for oneness from the nature of power rather than from scripture or authority, which makes it usable by anyone who accepts that real power does not stay passive. It also shows the Quran's characteristic move at the close: an argument is followed not by a summary but by a declaration of transcendence, so that the conclusion is worship rather than proof. What has been demonstrated logically is then removed from the reach of comparison.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same argument to a different end, the ruin of both heavens and earth.
Adds the third version, each god taking away what it created and overpowering the rest.
Continues the surah's concern with how God is named and how He is addressed.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the argument ends in praise, not in a scoreboard. Try that shape once today. When you finish thinking something through, whether it is a problem at work or a question you have been circling for weeks, do not stop at the conclusion. Add one sentence that is not an argument at all. The surah models a mind that reasons and then stops reasoning on purpose.

studies.title: A Praise You Cannot Hear
studies.meaning: Two ayat that seem unrelated and are not. The first says the seven heavens, the earth and everyone in them declare God's exaltedness, and then widens further: there is nothing at all that does not do so, though you do not grasp how. The second describes a curtain placed between the reciter and those who reject the hereafter. Read together, the universe is speaking and the barrier is on the listener's side.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch of the surah answering objections about other gods and about resurrection. The passage that follows describes coverings over the hearts of those who turn away and heaviness in their ears. Classical reports connect this section to opponents who would gather to listen to recitation at night and then mock it, though the details vary. The surah belongs to the years just before the migration.

keyTerms.note: The root means to swim or travel swiftly through something. The verb is not praise in general but the act of removing every unworthy thing from God, which is why a stone can do it by simply being what it is.
A verb for grasping the inner sense of something rather than merely hearing it. The ayah does not say the praise is inaudible; it says the failure is in the comprehension.
A name for the one who does not act on provocation at once. Placed at the end of an ayah about universal praise, it explains why those who withhold it are not immediately dealt with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sound carried a long way in the valleys around Mecca, and people were used to hearing things they could not place: wind through a gorge, a caravan bell before the caravan, the noise of a well being worked at night. A claim that everything was making a sound nobody could interpret was not strange to that audience. What was strange was being told the fault lay in their hearing.
studies.didYouKnow: The barrier in the second ayah is described with two words that both concern covering, one a curtain and the other meaning hidden, so it is a veil that is itself veiled. Commentators note that a barrier nobody can see is worse than one they can, because the person behind it does not know it is there.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first ayah makes worship the default condition of existence rather than a human speciality. Everything that exists already declares what God is by being what it is; the human being is the one creature that can decline. That reframes belief as joining something already in progress rather than starting it. The second ayah then locates unbelief in perception rather than in evidence, which is why the surah answers it with forbearance rather than with proof.

crossReferences.why: Birds in flight are said to know their own prayer and their own manner of praising.
Everything in the heavens and the earth prostrates, willingly or unwillingly, with its shadow.
Says the same recitation is healing for some and deafness for others.

studies.applyIt: Go outside tonight and stand still for one minute without your phone. Do not try to feel anything. Just list, silently, five things in front of you that were not made by a person. The ayah says each of them is already doing something you cannot hear. One minute is enough to notice how rarely you stop long enough to check.

studies.title: Say What Is Best
studies.meaning: The first ayah closes an argument about resurrection: on the day you are called, you will answer with praise, and the whole span of your life will look brief. Then the register changes completely. Servants are told to say the thing that is best, and a reason is given that is not about manners: Satan provokes friction between them. The commentators read the sequence as connecting the shortness of life to the pointlessness of quarrels.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage before it records opponents asking who would restore them once they were bones and dust. This one answers and then turns to the community itself. Classical reports connect the instruction about speech to friction between believers and those who abused them in Mecca, where an answer in kind would have cost more than it gained. The details of the reports differ.

keyTerms.note: A verb for a sudden goad or prick, the kind that starts a fight rather than sustains one. It suggests the first push rather than the argument, which is why the instruction addresses the opening sentence.
A superlative with the noun left out, so the phrase means the best of whatever is available to say. It does not ask for something acceptable; it asks for the top of the range each time.

A verb of remaining somewhere temporarily, used of a traveller stopping at a place. Applied to a whole life it frames the years as a halt on a journey, which is what makes the estimate come out short.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Words started wars in Arabia. A satirical verse against a clan could not be answered except by blood or by a better verse, and feuds lasting decades were traced back to a single insult at a well or a market. Reconciliation was the work of respected men who travelled between camps. In that setting, telling believers to say the best available thing was a strategy for survival as much as a virtue.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction is not given directly. God tells the recipient to tell My servants, so the command reaches its audience through a messenger and is framed by an expression of belonging. Commentators note that the same phrase, My servants, is used in the Quran at moments of particular tenderness, including the ayah about never despairing of God's mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A quarrel between believers is given a cause outside both parties. That is not an excuse, since the instruction still falls on the speaker, but it changes the diagnosis: the friction is being worked at from somewhere, so the first harsh sentence is the point of entry rather than the whole problem. Placing this immediately after a scene of resurrection also sets the scale. The dispute will look, from there, like part of a very short stay.

crossReferences.why: Push back with what is better, and an enemy may become a close friend.
Describes seeking refuge with God at the first prompting from Satan.
The same estimate on the Day: they whisper that they stayed only ten days, or one.

studies.applyIt: Pick the person you most often speak sharply to, and give yourself one rule for today: no first sentence that you would not want repeated back to you. Only the first sentence. That is where this ayah locates the problem, and it is small enough to actually hold for a day.

studies.title: We Honoured The Children Of Adam
studies.meaning: Four verbs, and the honour comes first. Human beings are dignified, carried on land and sea, provided with good things, and preferred over much of what was created. The commentators offer several grounds for the honouring: speech, reason, upright stature, the hand, the capacity to be addressed by God. Note the limit in the last clause, which says over many of those We created rather than over all, and the classical discussion turns on that word.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah arrives immediately after a passage about people who call on God at sea and forget Him on land, and just before a scene of the Day when every community is summoned. Placing an unqualified statement of human dignity between ingratitude and judgement is deliberate. The commentators report no specific occasion. The surah dates from the last Meccan years, when the community was small and despised.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb from the root for nobility and generosity. It describes conferring worth rather than recognising it, so the dignity is presented as given rather than earned or possessed by nature.
The verb for bearing a load. Applied to travel it credits the crossing itself to God rather than to the ship or the camel, which is a way of saying that mobility is also a gift.
A plural adjective used as a noun, covering food, and by extension whatever is clean and fit. The word marks quality rather than quantity, so the provision described is not simply abundance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Land and sea were the two ways out of Arabia and both were dangerous. Caravans crossed months of desert with camels that could be lost to thirst or theft; ships from the Red Sea ports ran with the season and sank often enough that a merchant family expected losses. To be carried on both was not a figure of speech. It named the two arrangements on which every Meccan fortune depended.
studies.didYouKnow: The honour is given to the Children of Adam, not to believers, so it covers every human being without condition. Classical commentators drew the point out explicitly, and it has been cited for centuries in discussions of how the dead and the enemy are to be treated. Nothing in the ayah is made to depend on faith or conduct.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Human worth is stated as a fact about God's action rather than as a conclusion about human qualities. That places it beyond argument and beyond forfeiture: nothing a person does can make them not a child of Adam. The qualification in the final clause is equally deliberate. Preference over many, rather than over all, leaves the ranking open and keeps the honouring from becoming a claim of supremacy over creation.

crossReferences.why: The angels are told to bow before Adam, the first form the honouring takes.
States the same dignity in the shortest form: made in the best of moulds.
Draws the consequence: one life taken unjustly counts as all of humanity.

studies.applyIt: Look for the person today whose work makes your day possible and whom you would normally not see: the cleaner, the driver, the one restocking the shelf. Say something to them that is not about the task. The ayah does not make the honour conditional on anything, and treating it that way costs about eleven seconds.

studies.title: An Entry Of Truth
studies.meaning: A prayer, a declaration, and a description. The prayer asks for an entrance and an exit that are both truthful, which the commentators read as any coming in and going out being sound at both ends, and many connect it to the migration ahead. The declaration announces that truth has arrived and falsehood is already vanishing, using a word for something that drains away. The third ayah says the same Quran works differently on different hearers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the last years there, immediately after instructions about the times of prayer and the night vigil. Many classical commentators connect the prayer about entering and leaving to the migration to Medina, and some report that the declaration about truth was spoken at the clearing of the sanctuary years later. The reports differ on the details, and the prayer is read more widely than any single occasion.

keyTerms.note: A construction that attaches truthfulness to a place or an act rather than to a statement. It asks that the coming in be honest in itself, without pretence at the start or regret at the end.
A verb used of a soul leaving the body and of something draining out. It does not mean falsehood was defeated; it means it emptied, which makes the collapse look internal rather than inflicted.
A medical word for recovery from illness. Commentators divide over whether the healing is of the heart, of doubt, or of the body, and most allow the range rather than narrowing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A person entering a town in Arabia did so under someone's protection or not at all, and leaving could be as dangerous as arriving. Travellers announced themselves, named their patron, and left with an escort to the edge of safe ground. Praying for a true entrance and a true exit used the vocabulary of that arrangement. It asked for the thing every traveller wanted: to arrive without deceit and to leave without disgrace.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for healing is used of the Quran in three places, and in every one it is paired with another quality: mercy here, mercy and admonition elsewhere, guidance in another. It is never left standing alone. The final clause of this passage is also carefully phrased: the Quran is not said to cause loss, only that the wrongdoers increase in it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The three ayat together give a shape to living under opposition. First a prayer for integrity in what you do, then a statement about what is already true regardless of appearances, then an account of why the same message divides its hearers. The last is the theologically striking one. Nothing in the Quran changes between the believer and the wrongdoer; what changes is what it meets, and the outcome is attributed to that.

crossReferences.why: Calls the Quran an admonition, a healing for what is in the chests, guidance and mercy.
Says the same book is guidance and healing for some and obscurity for others.
Describes truth hurled against falsehood so that it is crushed and vanishes.

studies.applyIt: Say the prayer in the first of these ayat before something you are dreading this week: a meeting, a hospital visit, a conversation. Ask for an honest way in and an honest way out. Then notice, afterwards, whether you left the room the same person who walked in. That is the specific thing the prayer is asking for.

studies.title: Whichever Name You Call
studies.meaning: Two instructions that look unrelated and share a subject. The first settles an objection: God and the Merciful are not two beings, and whichever name is used, the most beautiful names belong to Him. The second concerns volume in prayer, and asks for a way between loudness and silence. The commentators read both as answers to a single situation, where the words used in prayer were being overheard and made into an argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Classical sources report with reasonable agreement that some in Mecca objected to the name the Merciful, claiming not to know it, and used overheard recitation as material for mockery. Several commentators connect both halves of this ayah to that situation. The surah closes a few ayat later on the praise of a God who has no son, no partner and no ally out of weakness.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for the womb, so the name carries an encompassing, unearned tenderness. It is used in the Quran almost as a proper name, which is why the ayah can set it beside the other one.
A superlative feminine plural, so the phrase is not the good names but the best ones. The construction implies that no name reaches Him that is not at the top of its kind.
A verb for dropping the voice so far that it cannot be made out. Paired with its opposite in the same clause, it defines the instruction by two edges and leaves the middle unmeasured.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Prayer in Mecca was done wherever a believer could, often in the open near the sanctuary, and there was no privacy. Recitation carried, and passers-by stopped to listen or to jeer. Names mattered enormously in that culture: a person's name announced their lineage, and a god's name announced whose god it was. An argument about which name to use was an argument about whose the God being prayed to was.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah gives an instruction and declines to quantify it. Between loud and inaudible it says only to seek a way, leaving the level to circumstance rather than fixing it. Commentators have long noted this as a pattern in the Quran, where a range is set by its two ends and the judgement inside it is left to the person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The first half makes a point about language and God that goes further than the immediate dispute. Names are not containers; they are approaches, and no single one holds Him, which is why the plural is used and why it is qualified as the most beautiful rather than the complete. The second half then applies the same restraint to worship itself. A prayer pitched to be overheard, and a prayer hidden out of fear, are both being adjusted.

crossReferences.why: Names the same most beautiful names and says to call on Him by them.
Runs a long list of those names in three ayat, closing on their beauty.
Describes calling on your Lord humbly and in a low voice.

studies.applyIt: Try one prayer today at the volume this ayah describes: quiet enough that no one else in the room could take it down, loud enough that you can hear your own words. Most people pray either silently or performatively and have never tried the middle. It changes how much of the prayer you actually notice yourself saying.
